metadata.title: MCP, Explained
metadata.narration_disclosure: Narration is AI-generated (Kokoro am_onyx). The work, the configuration and the evidence shown are Saurabh K.'s.

beats.narration_text: Hi, I am Saurabh K., and this video is about M C P, the Model Context Protocol: what it is, and why it exists. One note before we start. The voice you are hearing is A I generated. The configuration, the servers and the evidence in this video are mine. Here is the question I want to answer.

props.command: A language model can only produce text. So how does it end up reading my files, driving my browser, and querying an API? Explain what MCP actually is, and why it had to be invented.

beats.narration_text: Here is the short version, before any detail. A model on its own is sealed in a box. It can only write text back to you. M C P is the standard plug that lets it reach outside that box, in a way you can see and switch off. That is the whole idea. The rest is how.

props.text:
MCP is a plugin system.
No, bigger than that.
One standard plug that lets
a model reach past its own
box — out in the open.

beats.narration_text: So what is it. Two sides, and the gap between them is the whole point. Everything your machine can do sits over here. The model sits over there, and it never crosses. All it can do is make a request. Whether that request turns into an action is a decision made on this side, every single time.

props.heading: A protocol with two sides
props.question: What is MCP?
lines: A CLIENT reads and calls them

beats.narration_text: Now why it had to exist. Before this, every app wired up every tool by hand. Ten apps and ten tools meant a hundred separate integrations, each one slightly different, each one breaking on its own schedule. One shared protocol turns that multiplication into addition. Write the server once, and every client that speaks M C P can use it.

props.heading: Multiplication becomes addition
props.lead: Every app wired every tool by hand.
lines: Write it once. Any client uses it.

beats.narration_text: Four words you will keep meeting. A host is the app you are using. A client is the connection it opens. A server is the thing offering the tools. And a tool is one callable action, with a name, a description, and a typed list of arguments. That last part is what makes any of this safe.

terms.meaning: The connection the host opens to a server
One action: a name, a description, typed arguments

beats.narration_text: This is not a diagram. This is my own configuration file, on this laptop, right now. Two servers. One called apify, reached over H T T P. One called rea, started as a local process on my machine. Same protocol, two different transports. That is the flexibility the standard buys you.

Open one of those tools and this is all it is. A name. A sentence saying what it does. And a schema listing the arguments, which are required, and what shape each one takes. The model reads this and nothing else. It cannot invent an argument the schema does not allow.

props.title: list_browser_targets.json
props.sparkLine: A name, a sentence, and a typed contract.

beats.narration_text: And here is that exact tool being called, earlier today, on this machine. One argument in. Five open browser tabs back, with their real titles. The model did not browse anything. It asked the server, the server looked, and the answer came back as plain data. Ask, then result. That is the entire loop.

props.title: call-and-result.json

beats.narration_text: So where does this help, and where should you be careful. It helps because the boundary is written down. You can read every tool a model was offered, and you can remove one. Be careful because a server you install runs on your machine with your permissions. Read what it declares before you trust it. The schema is the contract, and it is worth reading.

props.heading: The boundary is the feature
props.lead: You can read every tool it was given.
lines: LOOK TWICE — it runs as you

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Open whichever A I app you already use, find its M C P or connectors settings, and just read the list of tools it has been given. Do not add anything yet. Ask yourself one question for each one: do I understand what this is allowed to do. That is the habit worth building.

props.command: List every MCP tool this app currently has access to. For each one, show me its name, its description, and the arguments it accepts — and tell me plainly what it is allowed to do on my machine.
